planting.note: Root a callused stem-segment cutting in a chunky, fast-draining orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; like other named epiphyllum hybrids, King Midas flowers most dependably when kept a bit pot-bound rather than repotted into a large container.

directions: Grow in a coarse, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, with only mild early-morning sun tolerated outdoors. King Midas is a long-established named epiphyllum hybrid prized for its clear golden-yellow blooms, a comparatively rare flower color among the mostly pink-, red-, and white-flowered orchid cactus hybrids sold in the trade. Flowers open for a day or two in late spring or early summer on the broad, flattened, scalloped stems typical of epiphyllum hybrids. Water thoroughly and let the mix dry somewhat before watering again, feed with a diluted bloom-boosting fertilizer during active growth, and bring indoors or into a greenhouse well before frost, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in the mildest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a callused stem-segment cutting in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark or cactus mix in bright indirect light; Gusto, like most epiphyllum hybrids, sets buds more reliably when its roots are kept somewhat crowded in a modest-sized pot.

directions: Plant in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix and grow in bright indirect light, protecting from harsh midday sun that can scorch the flattened stems. Gusto is a classic named epiphyllum hybrid grown for its vivid, richly saturated red blooms, which open wide on arching, strap-like stems for a day or two in late spring or summer. Like other epicactus hybrids it descends from wild jungle cactus species such as Epiphyllum and Disocactus and does best with regular moisture during active growth, a slight dry-down between waterings, and light feeding with a bloom-boosting fertilizer while budding. Move to a frost-free spot well before winter, since it is reliably hardy outdoors only in zone 10-11.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a mature, callused stem cutting in a chunky orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; Padre produces some of the largest blooms among named epiphyllum hybrids, so give the flattened stems a sturdy stake or trellis for support as the plant matures.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, allowing only gentle morning sun outdoors. Padre is a well-known older epiphyllum hybrid valued for its exceptionally large, wide-petaled lavender-pink flowers that can rival dinner-plate size, opening for a day or two on broad, flat, scalloped stems in late spring or early summer. Feed lightly with a diluted bloom-boosting fertilizer through the growing season, water deeply and then let the mix dry somewhat before the next watering, and provide the same tropical-forest-canopy conditions of moderate humidity and filtered light that this jungle-cactus hybrid's wild ancestors enjoy. Protect from frost, since it is grown outdoors year-round only in the warmest zones and elsewhere as a container or greenhouse plant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings after a brief callusing period in a well-drained, chunky orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; this Central American species is one of the principal wild parents behind most large-flowered epiphyllum hybrids grown today.

directions: Grow in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark or cactus mix in bright indirect light, sheltering it from strong midday sun. Native to the forests of Guatemala and Honduras, this epiphytic species produces broad, wavy-margined, leaf-like stems and large, funnel-shaped, creamy yellow-white flowers that open at night and carry a strong, sweet fragrance, closing again by midmorning. It has long been used as a breeding parent for many of the larger-flowered named epiphyllum hybrids sold commercially, contributing size and fragrance to its offspring. Keep evenly moist but never soggy during the growing season, taper off watering in cooler months, and bring indoors or into a greenhouse well ahead of frost, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in the warmest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root callused stem-segment cuttings in a fast-draining orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; this Mexican cloud-forest epiphyte is one of the classic wild parents of red-flowered epiphyllum hybrids and prefers the same humid, filtered-light conditions.

directions: Plant in a chunky, well-drained orchid-bark or cactus mix and grow in bright indirect light, protecting the flattened, arching stems from direct midday sun. Native to cloud forests in Mexico and Guatemala, this epiphytic species bears brilliant scarlet-red, funnel-shaped flowers in spring that open by day rather than at night like many jungle cacti, making its bloom easy to enjoy without staying up late. It has been used for generations as a parent in hybridizing the red- and orange-flowered strains of orchid cactus sold commercially. Water thoroughly during active growth and allow the mix to dry somewhat between waterings, mist occasionally to raise humidity, and move to a frost-free location well before cold weather, since it survives outdoors year-round only in the mildest zones.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a callused stem-segment cutting in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; this historic cultivar, dating to the nineteenth century, still forms the flat, leaf-like stems typical of its Mexican species parent, Disocactus phyllanthoides.

directions: Grow in a coarse, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, shielding the flat, drooping stem segments from intense direct sun. Deutsche Kaiserin, meaning 'German Empress,' is one of the oldest named orchid cactus cultivars still commonly grown, producing abundant clear pink, funnel-shaped flowers in late spring that open by day and are smaller and more numerous than those of many modern large-flowered epiphyllum hybrids. Its parent species, native to Mexican forests, tolerates lower light and higher humidity than desert cacti and does best with consistent moisture during active growth, tapering off in winter. Bring indoors or into a greenhouse well before frost, since it is hardy outdoors year-round only in the warmest zones and elsewhere makes a floriferous hanging-basket or container specimen.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root small bundles of hair-thin stem segments after a brief callusing period in loose, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian forest epiphyte forms dense, cascading curtains of thread-like stems best displayed in a hanging basket.

directions: Grow in a loose, humus-rich, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light to light shade, misting occasionally to mimic the humid forest canopy this Brazilian epiphyte calls home. Its extremely fine, hair-like green stems branch repeatedly and cascade in soft, tangled curtains, giving it a texture unlike almost any other cactus and making it a favorite for hanging baskets where the trailing stems can spill freely. Tiny cream flowers appear along the stems in spring, followed by small translucent berries. Keep the mix lightly moist and never let it dry out completely for long, since this jungle cactus is far less drought-tolerant than desert species, but avoid waterlogging, which quickly causes stem rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a leaf-like stem segment after callusing for a few days in a well-drained, humus-rich orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this Brazilian epiphyte's broad, flattened pads often take on a reddish or purplish blush under stronger light.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, humus-rich orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light to light shade, allowing brief morning sun, which brings out a pink or bronze flush on the broad, flattened, leaf-like segments. Native to humid coastal forests of Brazil, this epiphytic cactus branches into stacked, wavy-edged pads that give mature clumps an almost succulent, wickerwork appearance, arching and drooping attractively over the rim of a hanging basket or elevated pot. Small pale flowers appear along the notched pad margins in fall or winter, followed by translucent pink to white berries. Water regularly enough to keep the mix from drying out completely, mist for humidity in dry indoor air, and avoid heavy, poorly drained soil that invites stem rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root short cuttings of the tiny, bead-like stem segments after a brief callusing period in gritty, well-drained orchid-bark mix in bright indirect light; this compact Brazilian epiphyte stays much smaller and denser than most of its Rhipsalis relatives.

directions: Plant in a gritty, well-drained, humus-rich mix and grow in bright indirect light to light shade, keeping this small epiphyte away from direct sun, which can scorch its fleshy, gray-green, button-like stem segments. Native to Brazilian forest canopies, it forms low, dense, slowly spreading mounds or short cascades quite unlike the long trailing stems of many other mistletoe cacti, making it well suited to a small hanging pot or a shallow dish alongside other epiphytic succulents. Tiny pale yellow-white flowers open along the stem tips in spring, followed by small white berries. Water moderately, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings, and protect from frost, since it thrives outdoors year-round only in the warmest zones and elsewhere is grown as a houseplant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Attach a rooted stem cutting flat against a piece of bark, cork, or a tree-fern slab wrapped in sphagnum moss in warm, humid, bright indirect light; in the wild this Amazonian epiphyte presses its flattened stems tightly against tree trunks and rarely roots into ordinary potting mix.

directions: Grow mounted flat against bark or a moss-wrapped slab in warm, humid, bright indirect light, since this remarkable Amazonian epiphyte naturally flattens its perforated, leaf-like stems directly against rainforest tree trunks, growing almost no visible spines or typical cactus form at all. Once mature, it produces an enormous, intensely fragrant white flower that opens for only a single night, closing again by dawn, a spectacle that has made it a favorite subject of nature documentaries filmed along Amazonian blackwater rivers. It demands consistently high humidity and warmth year-round and resents both direct hot sun and cool, dry indoor air, making it best suited to a warm greenhouse or terrarium rather than an ordinary houseplant setting. Keep the mounting medium lightly moist at all times rather than allowing the dry-down typical of most cacti, and expect several years of growth before the first flower appears.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
